How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

When imagining actions based on verbal movement instructions, maintaining an evolving mental representation across successive instructions is important. We examined this process from a working memory perspective, asking whether maintenance of verbally instructed action imagery depends on verbal working memory or can be sustained by action imageryrelated processes. In an adapted Final Position Judgment Task (FPJT), participants imagined three to six successive movements from listening to standardized movement instructions.

They then judged whether an image of a human figure matched their imagined final position.

Participants completed the FPJT in two conditions, once in baseline and once while repeating a syllable aloud to prevent verbal rehearsal. This articulatory suppression increased errors but performance remained above chance, suggesting that performance was not reducible to verbal rehearsal. Converging with this, FPJT errors were associated with visuospatial, but not verbal, working memory, with these associations not varying by FPJT condition. Articulatory suppression reduced reported verbal rehearsal and action imagery quality, whereas in both conditions, more than 80% reported visual rehearsal of instructed body parts to maintain imagery. Visual rehearsal was associated with fewer errors in baseline. Our results suggest that maintaining verbally instructed action imagery in the FPJT relies on action imageryrelated visual rehearsal and visuospatial working memory, with verbal rehearsal playing a supporting role. Given that FPJT performance also covaried with mental body rotation and mental paper folding performance, the FPJT appears suitable for assessing action imagery ability.

Introduction

The mental simulation of actions without physical execution (action imagery; Decety et al., 1989; Jeannerod, 1994) has attracted sustained scientific interest across disciplines and research areas. Fundamental research investigates the cognitive processes (Moran & O'Shea, 2020) and neural mechanisms (Hardwick et al., 2018) involved in action imagery, as well as its overlap with executed actions in physiological markers (Decety et al., 1991; Guillot et al., 2010) and temporal properties (Guillot et al., 2012; Guillot & Collet, 2005). These lines of work enhance our understanding of the contribution of action imagery to motor learning (Dahm et al., 2025) and its overlap with movement planning during action execution (Glover & Baran, 2017; Jeannerod, 2001). Applied research aims to translate related insights into practice by using action imagery to support motor rehabilitation and enhance athletes' performance (Holmes & Collins, 2001; López et al., 2019; Simonsmeier et al., 2021).

Accordingly, clarifying the mechanisms involved in action imagery is imperative for both theoretical and practical advances. Accumulating evidence indicates that action imagery draws on executive functions (Glover et al., 2020) and overlaps neurally with working memory (Van Caenegem et al., 2026). On a behavioral level, working memory was shown to mediate age-related differences in action imagery ability (Schott, 2012) and to be associated with outcomes of action imagery practice (Malouin et al., 2004). These findings may reflect both general cognitive demands and the role of working memory in maintaining and manipulating mental action representations.

Action imagery in the context of working memory

Action imagery (also referred to as movement imagery, motor imagery or action simulation; Moreno-Verdú et al., 2024) involves four processes (Cumming & Eaves, 2018; Kosslyn et al., 1995; Kraeutner et al., 2020): generation (creating a mental action representation), maintenance (keeping it active over time), manipulation (transforming or updating it), and inspection (evaluating its content). For example, imagining tossing and striking a volleyball involves generating an action representation of oneself, the volleyball and the environment. This action representation needs to be maintained and manipulated as the imagined action goes on. Ultimately, imagery inspection will determine whether the volleyball landed at the intended location. These processes situate action imagery within the framework of working memory, which provides the mental workspace for maintaining and manipulating information (E. K. Miller et al., 2018).

Working memory can be conceptualized as comprising multiple components (Baddeley et al., 2020; Baddeley & Hitch, 1974). These components are the central executive that allocates attention and resources, the phonological loop that maintains and manipulates verbal and auditory information (which we refer to as verbal working memory), the visuospatial sketchpad that maintains and manipulates visual and spatial information (which we refer to as visuospatial working memory), and the episodic buffer that integrates information across these components and long-term memory (for an alternative working memory conception, see Gade et al., 2014; Oberauer, 2009).

Working memory has been proposed to support the formation of mental models for action planning (Baddeley, 1993), and action imagery has been described as the internal rehearsal of motor acts within working memory (Decety & Grèzes, 1999). Yet, research on imagery and working memory has developed into two largely separate literature streams (Tong, 2013). This lack of literature integration is apparent for action imagery, whose functional relationship with working memory remains insufficiently understood (Moran & O'Shea, 2020) and sparsely considered in theoretical accounts (Hurst & Boe, 2022).

Therefore, clarifying how the verbal and visuospatial components of working memory are involved in maintaining action imagery is an important step towards integrating working memory and action imagery research.

Although action imagery can incorporate multiple sensory modalities, visual and kinesthetic imagery are typically emphasized (Krüger et al., 2022), with their relative contributions varying across task demands and individuals (Krüger et al., 2020). Combining visual and kinesthetic imagery can outperform visual imagery in systematic action imagery practice (Callow et al., 2017). They show partly distinct brain activation patterns (Lee et al., 2019), while recruiting a core network shared across imagery modalities (Van Caenegem et al., 2024). Below, we review research indicating that maintaining visual and kinesthetic information during action imagery can be linked to visuospatial and motor working memory: Visual imagery (not necessarily involving action) and visuospatial working memory, show similar neural patterns in the early visual cortex (Albers et al., 2013). Cognitively, visual imagery likely relies on maintenance and manipulation processes associated with visuospatial working memory (Baddeley & Andrade, 2000; Gyselinck et al., 2007; Keogh & Pearson, 2011; Sherwood & Pearson, 2010; Valenti & Galera, 2020), being sensitive to standard working memory manipulations (selective interference, set size). Visuospatial, but not verbal, interference reduces visual imagery vividness, whereas auditory imagery shows the opposite pattern (Baddeley & Andrade, 2000), and increasing set size (and thus working memory load) reduces imagery vividness, strength, and precision (Keogh & Pearson, 2017).

Moreover, even without explicit instruction, visual imagery can influence performance in visuospatial working memory tasks, as individuals with stronger sensory visual imagery show enhanced performance (Keogh & Pearson, 2011 , 2014; J. Pearson & Keogh, 2019).

Beyond visual information, action imagery involves mentally representing bodily

sensations (e.g., limb movement and position), whose temporary maintenance may draw on motor-related working memory (McDougle & Hillman, 2025). Recently executed motor acts are represented in the prefrontal and sensorimotor cortex (McDougle & Hillman, 2025), and individuals can maintain kinesthetic information of produced force (Vaillancourt & Russell, 2002) and reaching movements (Hillman et al., 2024; Jones & Henriques, 2010; Posner & Konick, 1966). Recall precision declines under standard working memory manipulations such as longer retention intervals (Adams & Dijkstra, 1966) and increasing set size (number of movements to remember; Hillman et al., 2024). Rather than relying on language-based representations only, the temporary maintenance of action instructions draws on motor-related representations: Recall improves when the instructed actions (e.g., touch a circle; spin a cross) are enacted during encoding or recall (Allen & Waterman, 2015), and when they are imagined during encoding rather than verbally rehearsed (Yang et al., 2024). These benefits of executing, anticipating or imagining instructed actions in maintaining and accurately recalling them are commonly interpreted as reflecting the formation of action plans that involve spatial-motoric coding (Allen & Waterman, 2015; Jaroslawska et al., 2016 Jaroslawska et al., , 2018;; Yang et al., 2024).

Taken together, this evidence points to a contribution of visuospatial and motorrelated working memory during visual and kinesthetic action imagery. Theoretical accounts differ in how motor coding is implemented within working memory. It could be embedded within visuospatial working memory (Allen & Waterman, 2015; Li et al., 2022), or a separate motor component (Jaroslawska et al., 2016 (Jaroslawska et al., , 2018;; McDougle & Hillman, 2025; Smyth & Pendleton, 1989; Vannuscorps & Caramazza, 2016). The existence of a motor working memory that incorporates both afferent (e.g., visuospatial and somatosensory input) and efferent (e.g., motor commands) information has recently been proposed (McDougle & Hillman, 2025). Accordingly, motor working memory maintains and manipulates motor content retrospectively, temporarily maintaining recently executed movements so that movement features can be integrated for refinement, and prospectively, supporting motor plans that precede actions and guide future behavior. Motor working memory can therefore serve as an internal buffer supporting imagery, manipulation, and rehearsal of future movements.

Such accounts delineate working memory processes in action imagery and can be integrated with theoretical accounts of action imagery, which have increasingly considered the role of working memory over recent decades. Early proposals emphasized a functional similarity between imagined and executed actions, focusing on shared motor representations and neural substrates (Jeannerod, 2001), with little attention to the cognitive resources required to maintain imagery over time. Subsequent frameworks introduced predictive internal models that explain how simulated actions generate and evaluate anticipated sensory consequences (Grush, 2004; Rieger et al., 2024), highlighting the need to maintain and compare action-related information during imagery. The motor-cognitive model (Glover & Baran, 2017) makes this reliance on cognitive control explicit by proposing that imagery and execution overlap during the planning phase but diverge during realization. Whereas action execution benefits from automatic online sensorimotor control, action imagery depends more heavily on conscious elaboration to construct and monitor the simulated action. Contemporary hybrid accounts of action imagery (for a discussion, see Hurst & Boe, 2022) propose a combined involvement of internal simulation and conscious monitoring. This aligns with the involvement of visuospatial and motor working memory processes.

The present study

In applied contexts, actions are systematically imagined to support motor rehabilitation (Dickstein & Deutsch, 2007; Kraeutner & Scott, 2025; López et al., 2019; McNeil et al., 2025). Such action imagery practice is often guided by verbal or written scripts (Holmes & Collins, 2001; Williams et al., 2013), which requires translating instructions accurately into mental action representations (Moran & O'Shea, 2020). Final Position Judgement Tasks (FPJT) closely match related demands by requiring participants to imagine an unfolding action according to successive verbal (written or auditory) movement instructions and judge whether an image of a human figure matches the imagined final position (e.g., Donoff et al., 2018; Madan & Singhal, 2013; Schott, 2013).

Such behavioral tasks provide a means to examine cognitive processes underlying action imagery (Decety et al., 1989; Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, McAteer, et al., 2025; Parsons, 1994). Action-related language can automatically engage the motor system (Pulvermüller, 2005) and may draw on motor representations shared with action imagery (Dupont et al., 2023). When imagining verbally instructed movements, participants may therefore imagine visual and kinesthetic sensations associated with the unfolding action. This may involve manipulating and maintaining visuospatial and motor-related representations in working memory. Given the required comparison with a visual stimulus (position judgement image), during action imagery, participants may shift their inner gaze between their body parts to maintain their position as the action unfolds (visual rehearsal).

Yet, responses in action imagery ability tasks can rely on processes largely independent of action imagery (e.g., Burte et al., 2019; Mibu et al., 2020). Lower sensorimotor expertise was shown to be associated with greater reliance on phonological representations rather than motor-related processing when remembering visually presented movement sequences (Moreau, 2013). Further, the modality of mentally represented information likely depends on its input modality (Allen et al., 2023). Thus, auditorily presented verbal instructions may be encoded phonologically and maintained through verbal rehearsal, demanding verbal working memory capacity. These considerations suggest two non-mutually exclusive rehearsal strategies in the FPJT: visual rehearsal to maintain the imagined body position, and verbal rehearsal to maintain the verbal movement instructions.

Visual rehearsal is therefore conceptualized as an action imagery-related rehearsal strategy, whereas verbal rehearsal may either support action imagery or enable final position judgements without its' use.

Against this background, we examined the contributions of action imagery and verbal rehearsal to final position judgements (see Table 1 for an overview of expectations). In the FPJT, participants listened to successive movement instructions and judged whether a subsequently presented image matched their imagined final position. We introduced two working memory manipulations: articulatory suppression (repeating a syllable aloud throughout the task) was supposed to selectively disrupt verbal rehearsal, and varying set size (from three to six movements) to manipulate working memory load. This allowed to examine how articulatory suppression affects maintaining verbally instructed action imagery, its associations with verbal and visuospatial working memory capacity and action imagery ability.

Because the FPJT requires processing auditory input, concurrently articulating a syllable could interfere with the initial phonological representation preceding the translation into visuospatial and motor-related representations (Yang et al., 2016). We therefore expected higher error rates and longer response times under articulatory suppression than at baseline. Such impairment would indicate disrupted verbal rehearsal (Baddeley, 2012; Christoffels, 2006; Larsen & Baddeley, 2003), supporting action imagery maintenance or serving as an alternative rehearsal strategy. Disrupted verbal rehearsal should be reflected in reported rehearsal strategy. Nevertheless, if final position judgements did not rely primarily on verbal rehearsal, performance should remain above chance under articulatory suppression.

More movement instructions were expected to increase working memory load because participants had to maintain the action imagery longer and compare more details with the position judgement image. We expected such set size-related effects to be reflected in higher error rates (Hillman et al., 2024) and longer response times (i.e., slower decision process; B. Pearson et al., 2014). Further, we examined the unique associations of verbal and visuospatial working memory capacity with errors in final position judgements to disentangle their contributions to task performance. Consistent with an action imagery process, we expected higher visuospatial working memory capacity to be associated with fewer errors in both conditions. Verbal rehearsal could support action imagery maintenance at baseline but should be impaired under articulatory suppression. We therefore expected higher verbal working memory capacity to be associated with fewer errors in the baseline condition only.

Additionally, we investigated whether the association between errors in final position judgements and visuospatial working memory capacity was stronger under articulatory suppression than in baseline. Such a pattern would be consistent with greater reliance on action imagery-related processing when verbal rehearsal is disrupted. Additionally, we expected to observe this shift in the reported frequencies of verbal and visual rehearsal.

Finally, as longer instruction sequences likely imposed higher working memory demands, we explored whether associations with verbal and visuospatial working memory capacity varied with the number of instructed movements.

We expected final position judgement performance to be positively associated with performance in other behavioral measures of action imagery ability, which engage processes of imagery manipulation (mental body rotation; Dahm et al., 2022) and maintenance (mental paper folding : Dahm & Draxler, 2022). These correlations were expected to be small to moderate in size, considering that measures of different action imagery processes correlate weakly to moderately (Czilczer et al., 2026; Kraeutner et al., 2020; Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, Van Caenegem, et al., 2025; Schott, 2013).

Reported rehearsal strategy in final position judgements was expected to be reflected in error rates and response times. Because visual imagery can support visuospatial task performance (Keogh & Pearson, 2011 , 2014; Moreau, 2012; J. Pearson & Keogh, 2019), and recall accuracy of action-related instructions is higher when participants use action imagery rather than verbal rehearsal (Yang et al., 2024), we expected reported visual rehearsal to correlate with lower error rates. Judging whether an image matches previously presented information is slower when that information is verbally compared to visually maintained (Reichle et al., 2000). This can be attributed to an additional recoding step such as translating the image into compatible propositional codes (Reichle et al., 2000). We therefore expected verbal rehearsal to be associated with slower responses.

Methods

Participants

We targeted a minimum sample size of N = 100 to provide sufficient power (> 80%) to detect the interaction between FPJT condition and Digit Span Task performance in a generalized linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) on FPJT trial errors (further including number of movements and the interaction between FPJT condition and Corsi Task performance; see Supplementary Material for details).

Participants were recruited from the experimenters' acquaintances and undergraduate Psychology students at the University of Innsbruck, who received course credits. Participation was voluntary. Of 135 participants, two did not complete the second session. Another 14 participants were excluded due to insufficient data quality, as defined by the following criteria, of which several applied to the same participants: needing more than three attempts on at least two of four comprehension checks, providing inconsistent responses (e.g., on the The final sample (76 female, 40 male, 3 diverse) was on average 25 years old (SD = 7.2; range = 19-63). Most participants were right-handed (112 right, seven left). All participants were native German speakers, reported having no hearing impairments, and normal or corrected to normal vision. Informed consent was obtained at the beginning of both sessions.

Setting

The experiment was implemented in OpenSesame 4.0.5 (Mathôt et al., 2012) and conducted in German. Data were collected in a one-on-one laboratory setting on a computer with a QWERTZ keyboard and over-ear headphones. The experiment file, including the auditory and visual stimuli of all behavioral tasks and the FPJT trial documentation, is available on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/nzfdc). Ethical approval was obtained from the Board for Ethical Questions in Science of the University of Innsbruck (reference number 03/2021).

Measures

Action imagery ability tasks

Final Position Judgement Task (FPJT). The FPJT presents an adaptation of similar tasks (Madan & Singhal, 2013; Naito, 1994; Nishida et al., 1986; Schott, 2013) that addresses previous limitations and enables standardized administration (in-lab and online) and comparability across settings. By using standardized verbal instructions presented auditorily (generated with Murf AI; https://murf.ai) at fixed intervals (see Fig. 1), the FPJT avoids written instructions, as used in earlier versions (Madan & Singhal, 2013 , 2014), that could be reread multiple times without time constraints. The adapted FPJT furthermore avoids spoken instructions (Schott, 2013) that may introduce experimenter effects. For participants relying on visual imagery rather than action imagery-independent processing, confounding irrelevant visual information can be particularly detrimental (Borst et al., 2012; Keogh & Pearson, 2014). The FPJT hence uses single-stimulus judgements rather than a stimulus selection out of multiple options, thereby providing precise measurement of response times alongside error rates. Note. (A) Example of an auditorily presented instruction sequence requiring participants to imagine assuming the starting position and performing five movements. The corresponding non-matching position judgement image depicts a backward step with the right leg instead of the instructed step to the side (correct response = "x" key). (B) Structure of each trial in the FPJT, involving three to six successive movements in the test block. (C) Overall FPJT procedure for baseline and articulatory suppression conditions.

In the FPJT, participants wore headphones and were instructed to close their eyes and imagine how it feels (kinesthetic imagery) and looks like (internal visual imagery) to execute the instructed movements from a first-person perspective. Within each trial (see Fig. 1B), the first instruction required participants to imagine assuming the starting position (i.e., upright standing position). Thereafter, each successive instruction required imagining a movement of a specific body part in a specific direction (in sum, 16 possible movements; see Table 2).

Trials comprised sequences of three to six movements, varying working memory demands 314 near proposed capacity limits (Cowan, 2001; Halford et al., 2007; G. A. Miller, 1956). The 315 inter-stimulus interval between instructions was set at 2s. After the last movement instruction 316 and a 2s interval, a tone (presented for 250ms) signaled participants to open their eyes. 317 Following a 2s fixation dot, a position judgement image (visual stimulus) was presented. The 318 image depicted a virtual human figure in a specific body position. This human figure was 319 shown from the back to avoid additional mental rotation demands and was positioned on an 320 orange position cross to facilitate orientation. Images were created in MPFB 2.0 BETA 2 321 (https://static.makehumancommunity.org/mpfb.html) in Blender (https://www.blender.org/), 322 using neutral physical appearance options. Participants judged as quickly and accurately as 323 possible whether the human figure's position matched their imagined final position by 324 pressing the "x" key for a non-matching and the "m" key for a matching stimulus using their 325 index fingers. For half of the trials, one body part that participants had been instructed to 326 imagine moving was depicted in the wrong direction (non-matching; see Fig. 1A). For the 327 other half of the trials, the instructions matched the human figure's final position (matching). 328 The image was presented on-screen until participants' response. 329 Note. Overview of the 16 possible movements instructed following the initial instruction to movement, direction) and order of movement instructions were balanced. Each body part was instructed only once per trial, and the second arm or leg was included only when head and upper body were also instructed within the same trial. Upper body instructions preceded arm and head instructions to minimize ambiguity.

The FPJT procedure (see Fig. 1C) started with a familiarization. In 16 familiarization trials (corresponding to the 16 possible movements, see Table 2) participants viewed an image of the virtual human figure after it had performed a single movement, starting from an upright standing position. Four written response options, corresponding to verbal movement instructions, were presented below the image. Participants selected the movement the human figure had performed. After responding, participants received feedback on whether their response was correct and listened to the audio corresponding to the correct response.

Following FPJT instructions and a comprehension check, participants completed four practice trials (two movements), with feedback on correctness and response time. The test block consisted of 32 randomly presented trials without feedback. Participants initiated each trial using the space bar. During the articulatory suppression condition, participants repeated the syllable "bla" (Padilla et al., 2005) from starting the trial (which started the auditory presentation of instructions) until pressing the "x" or "m" key to indicate their response. This aimed to suppress verbal rehearsal while listening to the movement instructions and while comparing the position judgement image with the action imagery.

Mental Body Rotation Task. To assess the association of the FPJT with a behavioral measure of mental rotation and perspective taking in action imagery (imagery manipulation), the Mental Body Rotation Task (Dahm et al., 2022; Steggemann et al., 2011) was administered. Participants viewed rotated human figures, facing forward or backward, and judged the laterality of an abducted limb (arm or leg) as quickly and accurately as possible (Fig. 2A). Stimuli were adapted from Dahm et al. (2022) by adding "action lines" to the abducted limb to reduce ambiguity in leg stimuli. Participants indicated which limb was abducted by responding with the "x" key (left index finger) for "left limb" and the "m" key (right index finger) for "right limb". They were instructed to imagine rotating their own body and abducting the respective limb from an internal visual perspective and to focus on kinesthetic sensations. The Mental Body Rotation Task comprised eight easy practice trials (0° rotation) with feedback and 40 trials in the test block presented in a balanced fixed order (45°, 135°, 180°, -135°, -45° rotation; no feedback). Each trial began with a fixation dot (one second), and the response triggered the next trial. (B) Note. (A) Example stimulus from the Mental Body Rotation Task showing a forward-facing figure rotated -45° with the right arm abducted (correct response = "m" key). (B) Example stimulus from the Mental Paper Folding Task showing five folds and three direction changes with overlapping lines (correct response = "x" key).

Mental Paper Folding Task. The Mental Paper Folding Task (Dahm & Draxler, 2022; Dahm & Sachse, 2025) was administered to assess the association of the FPJT with a behavioral measure targeting both imagery manipulation (spatial mental rotation) and imagery maintenance. Participants imagined folding a two-dimensional paper grid into a threedimensional cube using their hands, focusing on internal visual and kinesthetic sensations, and judged as quickly and accurately as possible whether two colored sides overlap (Fig. 2B).

Stimulus complexity varied by number of folds (three to five) and direction changes (zero to four). Participants responded with "x" (left index finger) for "no overlap" and "m" (right index finger) for "overlap". The task included four easy practice trials with feedback and 24 trials in the test block (balanced fixed order; no feedback), with each trial starting with a onesecond fixation dot.

Reported action imagery quality

Vividness of Movement Imagery Questionnaire 2 (VMIQ-2). The German version (Dahm et al., 2019) of the VMIQ-2 (Roberts et al., 2008) served to familiarize participants with action imagery, thereby assessing their subjective vividness of third-person external visual (M±SD = 3.7±0.7; Cronbach's α = .89), first-person internal visual (M±SD = 3.9±0.7; Cronbach's α = .92), and kinesthetic action imagery (M±SD = 3.8±0.7; Cronbach's α = .90) in 12 everyday actions (five-point rating scale:1 = no image at all, I only know that I am thinking of the skill;5 = perfectly clear and vivid; values from first session).

Action imagery quality items. To assess the subjective quality of participants' action imagery in the FPJT baseline (Cronbach's α = .82) and articulatory suppression condition (Cronbach's α = .84), and the relative involvement of sensory modalities, participants rated the ease and speed of imagery generation, imagery vividness, its maintenance and controllability, and the strength of visual imagery and imagined kinesthetic sensations on an eleven-point rating scale (0-10, with higher values indicating higher quality). These action imagery quality items were adapted from the Sport Imagery Ability Measure (Watt, 2003).

Working memory tasks

Digit Span Task. We applied the Digit Span Task to measure verbal working memory capacity. In this task, participants were required to maintain and recall sequences of auditorily presented digits ranging from 1 to 9. Digits were generated using Murf AI (https://murf.ai).

Each trial involved a sequence of two to nine digits (presentation duration ~ 500ms/digit, inter-stimulus interval of 600ms). Sequence length increased every two trials. Immediately after the final digit and a 600ms interval, a signal tone of 250ms cued participants to recall the digits aloud in the order presented. After a two-digit practice trial with feedback on whether the correct digits were recalled in the correct order, participants completed a test block consisting of 16 trials (no feedback). Digit order was balanced across trials. Performance was defined as the number of correctly recalled sequences (e.g., presenting 3-8-5-1 and recalling 3-9-5-1 was scored as incorrect).

Corsi Task. We applied the Corsi Task (Corsi, 1972; Sdoia et al., 2019) to measure visuospatial working memory capacity. In the Corsi Task, participants were required to maintain and recall sequences of illuminated squares. In each trial, participants were presented with ten blue squares on a black background, with their locations varying across trials. After an interval of 700ms, two to eight squares illuminated yellow for 700ms one after another. Sequence length increase every two trials. Immediately after the last square illuminated and a 350ms interval, a signal tone of 250ms cued participants to click the squares in the correct order, followed by feedback on whether the sequence was recalled correctly.

The task included a practice trial and 14 trials in the test block, with performance reflecting the number of correctly recalled sequences.

Procedure

Participants attended two sessions of approximately 50 minutes, spaced 7 to 14 days apart (Fig. 3) to reduce practice effects and mental fatigue. The order of the two sessions was counterbalanced across participants. Each session began with the VMIQ-2, after which either the FPJT baseline or articulatory suppression condition was completed. After the FPJT baseline condition, participants completed the Digit Span Task and the Mental Body Rotation Task. After the FPJT articulatory suppression condition, they completed the Corsi Task and the Mental Paper Folding Task. In both sessions, after completing the respective FPJT condition, participants indicated whether they had used (0 = no,1 = yes) visual rehearsal (mentally shifting gaze between instructed body parts to maintain imagery), and whether they had used verbal rehearsal (repeating instructions in inner speech). Visual and verbal rehearsal were coded independently, such that participants could also report using both strategies. Afterwards, they rated the task-specific action imagery quality items. Note. Participants completed either Session A or Session B first and completed the other session after an interval of 7-14 days. The order of Sessions A and B was counterbalanced across participants. VMIQ-2 = Vividness of Movement Imagery Questionnaire 2.

Data analysis

Outlier analysis

We excluded one FPJT item (three movement instructions) with atypically high error rates (≥ 3 SD; baseline: 63.87%; articulatory suppression: 68.07%), as the upper body rotation likely obscured detection of the incorrectly directed arm movement, making its construct validity questionable.

Data from participants performing below chance were removed for the respective behavioral task (Mental Body Rotation Task: n = 1; Mental Paper Folding Task: n = 7), likely reflecting incorrect key allocation. No univariate outliers (≥ 3 SD) were detected for the Digit Span Task or the Corsi Task. Univariate outliers in trial-level response times were removed (Mental Body Rotation Task: 1.3%; Mental Paper Folding Task: 1.8%; FPJT baseline: 1.8%; FPJT articulatory suppression: 1.0%).

Statistical approach

Response time analyses included trials with correct responses only, given that incorrect responses likely reflect different underlying processes (Ratcliff, 1978). Except for the GLMMs described below, inferential analyses were based on participant-level aggregated scores. Paired-samples t-tests were used to examine within-participant differences in continuous outcomes. Above-chance performance under articulatory suppression was assessed by comparing participants' error rates against the chance level of 50% using a onetailed one-sample t-test. Differences in the proportions of reported rehearsal strategies between conditions were examined using McNemar-tests. All correlations were Pearson correlations and included available data of all participants.

Significance was set at p < .05. Tests of differences in t-tests were one-tailed when corresponding to directional expectations and two-tailed otherwise. Because response times were descriptively shorter under articulatory suppression, contrary to our directional expectation, we report results of an exploratory two-tailed t-test. McNemar-tests, correlations, and GLMM coefficients were tested two-tailed. To control alpha inflation due to multiple ttests and correlations, p-values were adjusted family-wise using Bonferroni-Holm correction (e.g., across all correlations between performance measures in the FPJT and action imagery ability tasks).

GLMMs (level 1: FPJT trial, level 2: participant) were fitted using maximumlikelihood estimation with a Laplace approximation and a binomial logit link to examine the unique contributions of verbal and visuospatial working memory capacities to final position judgment errors (0 = correct,1 = incorrect), accounting for number of movements and potential interactions with FPJT condition. This multilevel approach was supported by a comparison of the intercept-only model with a random-intercept model, χ²(1) = 63.64, p < .001. Non-binary predictors were grand-mean centered, and binary predictors were effectcoded. Fixed and interaction effects were added stepwise based on theoretical expectations, with model selection guided by the Akaike information criterion (Akaike, 1974). Odds ratios were unstandardized and obtained by exponentiating the unstandardized logit coefficients.

Random effects were approximately normal, no overdispersion was detected, and residuals showed no systematic patterns, indicating that binomial GLMM assumptions were met.

Results

FPJT performance by condition and number of movements

The two performance indicators in the FPJT, error rates (% incorrect trials) and mean response times (correct trials in seconds), were approximately normally distributed (kurtosis ≤ 7 and skewness ≤ 2; e.g., Curran et al., 1996; Ryu, 2011) in the baseline (error rates: kurtosis = 2.69, skewness = 0.40; response times: kurtosis = 3.03, skewness = 0.64) and the articulatory suppression condition (error rates: kurtosis = 2.25, skewness = 0.16; response times: kurtosis = 2.59, skewness = 0.57). Error rates (r = .52, p < .001) and response times (r = .62, p < .001) correlated strongly between baseline and articulatory suppression conditions.

Error rates

As expected, performance under articulatory suppression remained above chance level (i.e., error rates significantly below 50%; 95% CI [18.3, 21.5]; t(118) = -36.92, p < .001), while error rates were significantly higher under articulatory suppression (M±SD = 19.9±8.9%) compared to the baseline (M±SD = 15.6±8.4%), t(118) = -5.49, p < .001, mean difference = 4.3%, 95% CI [-∞, -3], d = 0.50. This pattern held at each number of movements (see Fig. 4, full t-test results in Table A in the Supplement). movements Note. One-tailed paired samples t-tests with Bonferroni-Holm correction. * p < .05.

Within both FPJT conditions, error rates increased from three to four and from five to six movements, but not from four to five movements (Table 3), thus aligning partly with our expectations.

Response times 512

Contrary to expectations, when averaging across number of movements, response 513 times for correct trials were shorter under articulatory suppression (M±SD = 2.33±0.81 s) than 514 in the baseline (M±SD = 2.47±0.77 s), t(118) = 2.48, p = .01, mean difference = 0.14 s, 95% 515 CI [0.03, 0.25], d = 0.23. Self-reports by FPJT condition 540

In accordance with our expectations, fewer participants reported using verbal rehearsal 541 (i.e., inner speech) under articulatory suppression (33%) than in the baseline (60%), χ²(1) = 542 26.69, p < .001, φ = .48. Reported visual rehearsal (i.e., mentally shifting gaze between body 543 parts to maintain imagery) did not significantly differ between conditions (baseline: 83%; 544 articulatory suppression: 82%; χ²(1) = .05, p = .82), thus not supporting the expected greater 545 reliance on visual rehearsal under articulatory suppression. In both conditions, verbal rehearsal was rarely used without visual rehearsal (see Table 5). In the baseline condition, 547 participants most often reported combining verbal and visual rehearsal, whereas under 548 articulatory suppression, they predominantly reported visual rehearsal alone. Notably, eleven 549 participants reported visual rehearsal only in the baseline condition and nine only in the 550 articulatory suppression condition (equally distributed across order of conditions). 551 Additional analyses revealed significantly lower reported action imagery quality under 553 articulatory suppression than in baseline across all items (Table 6). In both FPJT conditions, 554 participants reported significantly stronger visual compared to kinesthetic imagery (baseline: 555 t(118) = 2.32, p = .02, mean difference = 0.7, 95% CI [0.1, 1.3], d = 0.21; articulatory 556 suppression: t(118) = 4.18, p < .001; mean difference = 1.4, 95% CI [0.7, 2.0], d = 0.38). 557

Associations between FPJT errors and working memory components

Pearson correlations revealed that FPJT error rates were significantly related to Corsi Task performance (baseline: r = -.30, p < .01; articulatory suppression: r = -.23, p = .03) but not to Digit Span Task performance (baseline: r = -.05, p = .57; articulatory suppression: r = -.13, p = .31). Converging with this pattern of results, a GLMM with trial-level error as the binary outcome and participant as a random intercept showed the best fit when including fixed effects of FPJT condition, number of movements, and Corsi Task performance (Table 7; model comparisons in Supplement Table C). Adding Digit Span Task performance (range = 5-15; M±SD = 10.01±1.99) to the model did not improve model fit. Compared to the baseline, articulatory suppression significantly increased error odds by 36%. Further, each additional movement significantly increased error odds by about 26%, and each additional point on the Corsi Task (range = 6-13; M±SD = 9.53±1.39) significantly decreased error odds by about 11%, aligning with expectations. We specified in our expectations that if FPJT errors were primarily driven by verbal working memory, we should observe an association between lower odds of an FPJT error and participants' Digit Span in the baseline condition, but not under articulatory suppression. A corresponding shift in strategy would further be supported if the association between lower FPJT error odds and Corsi Task performance was stronger under articulatory suppression than in baseline. Neither interaction was significant, and neither Digit Span nor Corsi Task performance effects on errors interacted with the number of movements.

Associations between performance in FPJT conditions and action imagery ability tasks

In line with expectations, FPJT error rates and response times correlated significantly with the respective error rates and response times in the Mental Body Rotation Task (error rates baseline: r = .27, p = .01; error rates articulatory suppression: r = .22, p = .04; response times baseline: r = .33, p < .01; response times articulatory suppression: r = .4, p < .001) and Mental Paper Folding Task (error rates baseline: r = .26, p = .02; error rates articulatory suppression: r = .22, p = .04; response times baseline: r = .31; response times articulatory suppression: r = .30, ps = .01). The Mental Body Rotation Task and Mental Paper Folding Task correlated significantly in response times (r = .30, p < .01), but not in error rates (r = .19, p = .18). Correlations of FPJT performance with general imagery vividness (VMIQ-2) and FPJT-specific action imagery quality ratings are reported in Supplementary Table D. VMIQ-2 ratings were unrelated to FPJT performance. Among FPJT-specific ratings, lower baseline error rates were significantly associated with higher imagery maintenance ratings. Under articulatory suppression, lower error rates were significantly associated with higher ratings on all items. Action imagery quality was unrelated to response times.

Associations between performance in FPJT conditions and reported rehearsal strategy

Reported visual rehearsal correlated significantly with lower error rates (r = -.23, p = .04) in the baseline condition only (articulatory suppression: r = -.17, p = .14), aligning partially with expectations. Reported verbal rehearsal did not significantly correlate with response times (baseline: r = .19, p = .13, articulatory suppression: r = -.04, p = .65).

Exploratory correlations revealed that in both conditions, reported verbal rehearsal was unrelated to FPJT error rates (baseline: r = -.06, p > .99, articulatory suppression: r = 0, p > .99), and reported visual rehearsal was unrelated to response times (baseline: r = .09, p = .98, articulatory suppression: r = .14, p = .52). Correlations of reported rehearsal strategy with the VMIQ-2, Mental Body Rotation Task and Mental Paper Folding Task are reported in the Supplement (Table E). Reported visual rehearsal in the baseline condition was significantly positively correlated with kinesthetic imagery vividness in the VMIQ-2, whereas all other correlations were non-significant.

Discussion

The present study examined the contributions of action imagery and verbal rehearsal to maintaining verbally instructed action imagery. Participants completed an adapted FPJT under baseline and articulatory suppression conditions, with articulatory suppression serving as a selective interference manipulation targeting verbal rehearsal. In line with expectations, under articulatory suppression, error rates increased relative to baseline, while performance remained above chance. Response times tended to increase with the number of instructed movements (i.e., set size effect), consistent with increasing working memory load. Contrary to expectations, however, participants responded faster under articulatory suppression than in baseline, primarily for longer movement sequences. Corsi Task performance, but not Digit Span Task performance, was associated with fewer final position judgement errors, partly consistent with our expectations. While under articulatory suppression, reported use of verbal rehearsal was expectedly reduced, reported use of visual rehearsal did not increase. Neither association differed significantly between FPJT conditions. In line with expectations, FPJT performance was positively associated with performance in behavioral action imagery ability tasks. In the baseline condition, reported visual rehearsal was associated with lower error rates.

Contributions of action imagery and verbal rehearsal to final position judgements

The performance decline under articulatory suppression is consistent with the assumption of an initial phonological representation (Allen et al., 2023) and the loss of verbal rehearsal support in remembering movements (Xie et al., 2021). Performance remained above chance under suppression, suggesting that final position judgements also involved processes beyond verbal rehearsal. Further, although more than half of the participants reported verbal rehearsal at baseline, the overall pattern of findings indicates that it supported the maintenance of action imagery rather than drove performance.

First, strong correlations across baseline and articulatory suppression for both error rates and response times indicate substantial stability in individual performance and are consistent with shared processes contributing to both conditions. Second, a high proportion of participants reported visually rehearsing body parts during imagery in both FPJT conditions, suggesting reliance on action imagery-related processes irrespective of selective interference with verbal rehearsal. Third, visuospatial working memory capacity (approximated via Corsi Task performance), but not verbal working memory capacity (approximated via Digit Span Task performance), was related to fewer errors in final position judgments.

More specifically, individual differences in verbal working memory capacity did not account for additional variance in final position judgement errors, irrespective of articulatory suppression and the number of movements. Although verbal working memory can support the retention of verbal instructions (Baddeley & Hitch, 2019; Yang et al., 2016), the present findings provide no evidence that its capacity meaningfully supported final position judgements. By contrast, higher visuospatial working memory capacity was associated with fewer errors across conditions, pointing to modality-specific processes rather than working memory capacity in general. This interpretation aligns with evidence that visual imagery relies on maintenance and manipulation processes associated with visuospatial working memory (Baddeley & Andrade, 2000; Keogh & Pearson, 2011; Sherwood & Pearson, 2010; Valenti & Galera, 2020), which also support action imagery (Schott, 2013). Visual imagery thus likely contributed to maintaining action imagery generated from verbal instructions both at baseline and under articulatory suppression. Converging neurophysiological evidence for action imagery involvement comes from an earlier FPJT, in which correct trials showed stronger mu suppression than incorrect trials, consistent with sensorimotor involvement in successful action imagery (Chen et al., 2021). Finally, reported visual, but not verbal, rehearsal was associated with fewer errors at baseline. This finding aligns with evidence that action imagery-related processing supports the maintenance of movement instructions more effectively than verbal rehearsal (Yang et al., 2024).

Further evidence for the involvement of action imagery in both conditions comes from the observed positive associations between performance in the FPJT and action imagery ability tasks. Even when verbal rehearsal was not disrupted, final position judgments captured aspects of action imagery ability that overlap, but are not identical, to those assessed in mental body rotation and mental paper folding. Unlike final position judgments, which require participants to generate action imagery from auditory input, manipulate and maintain it, and then compare it with an image, mental body rotation and mental paper folding elicit action imagery directly from visually presented stimuli. Generating imagery "from scratch" in final position judgments likely places greater demands on imagery generation, maintenance, and inspection. This may account for the small to moderate correlations, given similarly sized associations among behavioral tasks capturing different action imagery processes (Kraeutner et al., 2020; Moreno-Verdú, Waltzing, Van Caenegem, et al., 2025; Schott, 2013) and evidence that earlier FPJT versions did not correlate with a mental object rotation task that did not involve an actor (Madan & Singhal, 2013).

Because participants needed to translate verbal instructions into mental action representations, as in script-guided action imagery (Moran & O'Shea, 2020), articulatory suppression may also have impaired action imagery itself. This is consistent with lower FPJTspecific action imagery quality ratings than at baseline and evidence that task-irrelevant auditory input can disrupt action imagery (Hohmann et al., 2016). Yet, FPJT-specific action imagery quality ratings corresponded more consistently with accurate final position judgements under articulatory suppression. This may reflect greater reliance on action imagery when verbal rehearsal was disrupted. However, as errors were unrelated to verbal working memory capacity, the pattern might indicate greater awareness of imagery limitations under higher task demands. Given the susceptibility of self-evaluations to self-enhancement (Alicke et al., 1995; Alicke & Sedikides, 2009), FPJT-specific ratings may reflect both subjective action imagery quality and experienced task difficulty.

Set size and response time patterns in the Final Position Judgement Task

In both conditions, error rates and response times tended to increase with working memory load, manipulated via number of movements. This set size effect is consistent with working memory involvement in maintaining action imagery (Baddeley, 2012; Cowan, 2001; Dunham et al., 2020; B. Pearson et al., 2014). Consistent with most participants reporting visual rehearsal of body parts in a serial manner, the response time pattern suggests a serial comparison process by imagined body part rather than a holistic visual inspection (Hegarty, 2004). Participants likely performed a self-terminating serial comparison process, as identifying matching stimuli was slower than identifying non-matching stimuli. In that case, detecting a non-matching position of a body part terminates the comparison of the presented image with one's imagery earlier than confirming a fully matching image.

One explanation for shorter response times under articulatory suppression, compared to the baseline, is an increase in task demands during the response phase due to the sustained repetition of "bla". This, potentially effortful, articulatory suppression might have induced a shift toward prioritizing speed over accuracy, consistent with speed-accuracy trade-off mechanisms under increased cognitive load (Alister et al., 2024; Heitz, 2014). Because action imagery was more difficult to maintain under articulatory suppression, participants may have responded more quickly before it decayed further. Additionally, articulatory suppression induced a rhythm to the task which may have contributed to faster responding.

Limitations and outlook

Because the FPJT requires judging an image of a human figure, internal visual imagery was expected to be a core task demand (Krüger et al., 2022). This motivated inclusion of the Corsi Task to test whether visuospatial maintenance accounts for unique variance in final position judgment errors beyond variance associated with maintaining verbal information (Digit Span Task). Corsi Task performance was indeed associated with fewer errors, but the association was rather weak. This may partly reflect the FPJT requirement to repeatedly update, rather than simply maintain, the imagined body position. Future studies could therefore examine associations between performance in the FPJT and in tasks requiring working memory updating. Beyond these manipulation demands, additional variance may arise from other maintenance processes not captured by our study. Participants may have kinesthetically rehearsed the body position by repeatedly imagining movement-and posturerelated sensations (e.g., heaviness in a raised arm, stretch in the calf of a backward-extended leg, tension in the neck given the upwards lifted head). Such a rehearsal strategy is plausible because the movement instructions likely engaged the motor system (Dupont et al., 2023), and participants were asked to use (and also reported) internal visual and kinesthetic action imagery. Therefore, future studies could include a measure of motor working memory capacity to examine whether it explains variance in FPJT performance beyond visuospatial working memory capacity.

Although these considerations suggest that the FPJT involves action simulation, based on the behavioral data, the present study cannot rule out the possibility that participants solved the task using visual mental imagery detached from action imagery. Selective interference paradigms comparing visuospatial and motor suppression could help determine the specific contribution of motor-related representations to FPJT performance. Articulatory suppression inevitably involved mouth movements, which may have introduced motor interference. This provides an additional account of impaired performance under articulatory suppression.

However, because these movements were task-irrelevant and relatively simple, substantial motor suppression effects appear unlikely. In addition to selective interference paradigms, future studies could ask participants about a broader range of rehearsal strategies. Yet, these self-reports are limited by their reliance on participants' conscious access to their strategy use.

Finally, the relative contribution of action imagery-related processes and verbal rehearsal likely depends on task demands (Chrysikou et al., 2014; Paivio, 1969). Future studies could examine whether action imagery-related processes still contribute more than verbal rehearsal to maintaining action imagery when the presentation of movement instructions is self-paced.

Overall, our findings suggest that the FPJT engages action imagery and that imageryrelated visual rehearsal benefits task performance. Together with the absence of an association between errors in final position judgements and verbal working memory capacity, the FPJT may be a suitable measure of aspects of action imagery ability that are relevant for action imagery practice guided by verbal instructions. Earlier FPJT versions have already been used as behavioral measures of action imagery ability (e.g., Lambert et al., 2023 Lambert et al., , 2024 Lambert et al., , 2025;; Muraki & Pexman, 2021; Schott, 2012; Schott et al., 2021). Ready-to-use OpenSesame and PsychoPy versions of the FPJT are available for local and online testing, with options to customize language, response mode (unimanual or bimanual), and feedback: https://github.com/carlacz/FPJT.

Conclusion

Taken together, our findings point to a greater contribution of action imagery-related processes than of verbal rehearsal to maintaining verbally instructed action imagery. This interpretation is supported by above-chance performance under articulatory suppression and by the finding that visuospatial working memory capacity supported correct final position judgements, but verbal working memory capacity did not. Visual rehearsal was widely reported in both conditions, suggesting reliance on action imagery-related processes already at baseline rather than a compensatory shift under articulatory suppression. Given that visual rehearsal, but not verbal rehearsal, was associated with better FPJT performance, and that FPJT performance correlated with behavioral action imagery ability tasks, the FPJT appears suitable for assessing action imagery ability.
